posts.text: Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.
Ultrastable is an autonomous system that sets up and runs any organized effort from one idea.
Ultrastable runs the system: it turns an idea into a managed, self-improving organization.
Agents are cheap now; managing them is the hard part.
You give it an idea and it sets up the roles, does the work, checks it, and reports in four lines a day.
Most people with a good idea never get past the overhead: product, brand, licensing, a search presence, marketing.
AI agents can now do the work, but they leave the manager's job undone.
Give it an idea and it stands up the whole set of roles, plans the work, does it, verifies it and reports back briefly.
Ultrastable decides what needs doing, checks the results and reports.
An autonomous system that turns an idea into a running organization.
Agents are cheap; managing them is the bottleneck.
Ideas die in the overhead of product, brand, legal protection, search presence and marketing.
Give it an idea; it sets up the roles, plans the work, does it, checks it and reports.
Coding agents write code; Ultrastable runs the system around the code.
Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.
Ultrastable is an autonomous system that sets up and runs any organized effort from one idea.
Ultrastable runs on itself. Its own planning, work tracking and reporting are run by the system it gives to others.
A system is something else: many agents, each with one job, running in code loops that check and improve their own work, with the rules written as code too.
That is how Ultrastable is built: multi-agent, self-referential loops, not a single code agent.

texts.linkedin:
Closing the loop: Ashby's ultrastable system and why today's AI systems disappoint

A common belief: AI systems are smart enough already; what holds them back is model capability.

What holds most AI systems back is an open loop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails. That is an engineering property, and it can be tested.

What the system's own records show (window of 0.75 days, 64 merged changes):
• Share of declared essential variables that have limits: 1.0 (n = 11) against a target of >= 1.0 (met).
• Second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days: 17 (n = 466) against a target of >= 1 (met).
• Share of essential variables whose second loop can change a parameter of the first loop: 0.273 (n = 11) against a target of >= 0.5 (not met yet).
• Share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner: 1.0 (n = 105) against a target of >= 1.0 (met).

3 of 5 tests met; every miss is an open work item. The paper regenerates itself from the records after every change, limits included.

Why this is on my feed: Ultrastable runs on Ultrastable. Its fixes, deploys and these white papers are produced and checked by the system itself, from its own records. Practical Solutions is one example of a system it runs: a free, evidence-based catalogue of fixes for global problems that keeps its own evidence current. The subject is the example; the point is what a self-running system can do for your own work. https://ultrastable.org

Full paper, method and limits: https://ultrastable.io/research/ashby-1952

Review without a queue: what Chen and Stratton (2026) mean for an autonomous system

A common belief: AI writes more code, so a team must review more code, and review becomes the bottleneck.

Review is a bottleneck only when a person is the gate. Replace the queue with checks that can fail, live verification and automatic revert, and measure quality instead of waiting.

What the system's own records show (window of 0.75 days, 64 merged changes):
• Verified live deploys per merged pull request in the same window: 0.625 (n = 64) against a target of >= 0.5 (met).
• Median hours from a pull request opening to its merge: 0.15 (n = 64) against a target of <= 1.0 (met).
• Median hours to merge for pull requests the system's own workflows or App opened: 0.49 (n = 13) against a target of <= 2.0 (met).
• Share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself: 0.203 (n = 64) against a target of >= 0.5 (not met yet).

5 of 7 tests met; every miss is an open work item. The paper regenerates itself from the records after every change, limits included.

texts.linkedin:
Closing its own loops: what an AI system that runs itself shows about the human in every step

A common belief: AI agents can draft code, but a person still has to merge it, deploy it and check that it works.

Merging, deploying and checking are loops, and loops can be closed by code: checks that can fail, a lane that merges what passes, a probe that proves the deploy live, and a revert when it is not.

What the system's own records show (window of 7.87 days, 359 merged changes):
• Share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner: 1.0 (n = 117) against a target of >= 1.0 (met).
• Median hours from a pull request opening to its merge: 0.13 (n = 359) against a target of <= 1.0 (met).
• Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit: 0.999 (n = 890) against a target of >= 0.95 (met).
• Human touches counted by the latest criticality tick: 0 (n = 0) against a target of <= 0 (not measured yet).

3 of 6 tests met; every miss is an open work item. The paper regenerates itself from the records after every change, limits included.
